observation_summary: The StringUtils methods fail to correctly handle Unicode supplementary characters (surrogate pairs), leading to incorrect results in containsAny, containsNone, and indexOfAny/But methods. The tests confirm that these methods treat surrogate pairs as individual characters, causing false positives/negatives.
hypothesis: The StringUtils methods (containsAny, containsNone, indexOfAny, indexOfAnyBut) iterate over the input string using char-by-char processing (e.g., using charAt(i)), which incorrectly splits Unicode supplementary characters (represented as surrogate pairs in Java) into two individual 16-bit chars. This causes the methods to incorrectly match or mismatch based on partial surrogate components rather than the full Unicode code point.
prediction: The implementation of these methods in StringUtils will show loops that iterate over the string using index increments of 1 and perform comparisons on individual chars, failing to account for Character.isSupplementaryCodePoint or Character.codePointAt.
experiment_rationale: The failure patterns in the provided tests (e.g., failing to distinguish between supplementary characters and their individual surrogate components) strongly indicate that the underlying algorithm is performing character-level iteration instead of code-point-level iteration.
reasoning_summary: The bug is a classic case of incorrect handling of Unicode supplementary characters in Java. The methods in StringUtils are designed to work with char arrays or strings, but they iterate using charAt(i), which is insufficient for characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). The fix requires updating the iteration logic to use code points (e.g., Character.codePointAt) to correctly identify and process surrogate pairs.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: While the fix involves adding checks for surrogate pairs, the root cause is the fundamental algorithmic approach of iterating by char instead of code point.
